questions.q: Arrange in increasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition: ethanal, propanal, propanone, butanone.
questions.explain: Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes (more hindrance, two electron-releasing groups), and within each class the larger alkyl group lowers reactivity further.

questions.q: Which aldehyde is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
questions.explain: The nitro group withdraws electrons by −I and −R effects, making the carbonyl carbon more positive; –CH₃ and –OCH₃ donate electrons and lower reactivity.

questions.q: Arrange towards HCN addition in increasing reactivity: acetaldehyde, acetone, di-tert-butyl ketone, methyl tert-butyl ketone.
options: Acetaldehyde < acetone < methyl tert-butyl ketone < di-tert-butyl ketone
Di-tert-butyl ketone < acetone < methyl tert-butyl ketone < acetaldehyde
Di-tert-butyl ketone < methyl tert-butyl ketone < acetone < acetaldehyde
Methyl tert-butyl ketone < di-tert-butyl ketone < acetaldehyde < acetone
questions.explain: Steric hindrance dominates: each tert-butyl group blocks the approach of CN⁻, and di-tert-butyl ketone barely reacts at all.

questions.q: CH₃MgBr (1 equivalent) is added to a compound containing both a free –COOH group and a ketone C=O. The first reaction is:
options: Deprotonation of –COOH, giving RCOO⁻MgBr⁺ and methane
Nucleophilic acyl substitution at the –COOH group, giving a methyl ketone
Nucleophilic addition to the ketone C=O, giving a tertiary alkoxide
Coupling at the carbon next to the C=O by SN2
questions.explain: A Grignard reagent is a strong base, so any acidic hydrogen reacts first and RMgX is destroyed as R–H; a free –COOH does not undergo acyl substitution with RMgX, it simply protonates it.
